questions.prompt: A join:
choices: Sorts a table by a column
questions.explain: An attribute join matches a shared key; a spatial join matches by location.

questions.prompt: The shared column used to match rows in an attribute join is the:
questions.explain: For example, a student ID or a county FIPS code.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps only the rows whose key appears in both tables?
questions.explain: Unmatched rows on either side are dropped.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps every row of the first table and adds matching columns from the second?
questions.explain: Rows with no match get NA in the new columns.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps every row from both tables?
questions.explain: It fills NA wherever a row has no match.

questions.prompt: Any right join can be rewritten as a left join by swapping the order of the tables.
questions.explain: students |> right_join(takes) keeps the same rows as takes |> left_join(students).

questions.prompt: A left join returns more rows than its left table. Why?
choices: Some keys match more than one row in the right table
The right table had missing values
Left joins always add one row
questions.explain: A one-to-many match copies the left row once for each match.

questions.prompt: After `students |> left_join(takes, by = join_by(id))`, a student who took no courses:
choices: Appears once, with NA in the course columns
questions.explain: A left join never drops a row from the left table.

questions.prompt: What does `by = join_by(id)` do?
choices: Names the key column to match on
questions.explain: Without it, dplyr joins on every shared column name and prints a message.

questions.prompt: Why can a natural join be risky?
choices: It matches on every column with the same name, even ones you didn't intend
It always returns a cross join
It only works on spatial data
questions.explain: If both tables also had a `name` or `year` column, it would silently join on those too.

questions.prompt: A cross join of a 4-row table and a 5-row table has how many rows?
questions.explain: A cross join pairs every row with every row: 4 × 5 = 20.

questions.prompt: How do you combine three tables with dplyr?
choices: Pipe the result of one join into the next
List all three in one join_by()
You can't; joins take only two tables
questions.explain: students |> inner_join(takes, ...) |> inner_join(instructor, ...).

questions.prompt: Cardinality describes:
choices: How many rows in one table can match a row in the other
The number of columns in a table
The coordinate system of a layer
questions.explain: Know it before you join, so you know how many rows to expect.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinality between governors and states?
questions.explain: Each state has one governor, and each governor governs one state.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinality between students and classes?
questions.explain: Each student takes many classes, and each class has many students.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinality between capital cities and states?
questions.explain: Each state has one capital, and each capital belongs to one state.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinality between a state and its cities?
questions.explain: One state has many cities. Seen from the cities' side, it is many-to-one.

questions.prompt: When do you need a spatial join instead of an attribute join?
choices: When the tables share no key column, only location
When the tables have the same number of rows
When one table is a raster
questions.explain: EMS calls and neighborhoods share no ID; the only link is where each call happened.

questions.prompt: In `st_join(x, y)`, which layer receives the new attributes?
questions.explain: x is the destination and y the source, like the left table of a left join.

questions.prompt: By default, `st_join()` behaves like which attribute join?
questions.explain: It keeps every row of x. Set left = FALSE for an inner join.

questions.prompt: Which `join` argument attaches the closest feature?
questions.explain: Then use st_distance() to find how far away it is.

questions.prompt: Counting the schools in each county is a:
questions.explain: Counties are the destination; all the schools inside each one are aggregated into a count.

questions.prompt: Attaching the county each school is in is a:
questions.explain: Each school is in exactly one county, so there's no ambiguity: many-to-one.

questions.prompt: In R, a summarized spatial join is usually `st_join()` followed by:
questions.explain: Aggregate the matches for each destination feature, then attach the result.

questions.prompt: A distance join on data in latitude and longitude returns distances like 0.47. What units are these, in most GIS software?
questions.explain: Distances come out in the data's units. Project first.

questions.prompt: A nearest-feature join can attach a different feature when run on latitude and longitude than when run on projected data.
questions.explain: Degrees stretch unevenly, so nearest in degrees isn't always nearest on the ground.

questions.prompt: Before a distance join, you should:
choices: Check both layers with st_crs() and project them with st_transform()
questions.explain: Use a projection that preserves distance in your study area, such as NC State Plane.

questions.prompt: Base R's `merge()` joins two data frames. Store an inner join of `a` and `b` on the column `id` in `ab`.
questions.starter:
a <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy"))
b <- data.frame(id = c(2, 3, 3, 4), course = c("GEOG", "MATH", "HIST", "ART"))
questions.solution:
a <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy"))
b <- data.frame(id = c(2, 3, 3, 4), course = c("GEOG", "MATH", "HIST", "ART"))
ab <- merge(a, b, by = "id")
questions.explain: merge(a, b, by = "id") is an inner join: Ben once, Cy twice. Add all.x = TRUE for a left join.

questions.prompt: Store a left join of `a` and `b` on `id` in `ab`, keeping every row of `a`. (Hint: `merge()` has an `all.x` argument.)
questions.starter:
a <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy"))
b <- data.frame(id = c(2, 3, 3, 4), course = c("GEOG", "MATH", "HIST", "ART"))
questions.solution:
a <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy"))
b <- data.frame(id = c(2, 3, 3, 4), course = c("GEOG", "MATH", "HIST", "ART"))
ab <- merge(a, b, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
questions.explain: Ana has no course, so she appears once with NA; Cy appears twice. That's 4 rows.
